name: 2 Kings
author: The writer of 2 Kings is not named; 1 and 2 Kings were originally one book. Jewish tradition credits the prophet Jeremiah. Many scholars instead see it as the work of unnamed editors, possibly priests or scribes, who shaped a larger history running from Deuteronomy through Kings, perhaps with a first edition under King Josiah and a final one during the exile. Either way, the writer drew on older royal records and stories of the prophets, some of which are named in the book.
audience: The finished book was first read by Jewish people after the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC (some date it 587), many of them living as exiles in Babylon and others among the ruins at home. With no king, no temple and no land of their own, they were asking how their nation had come to fall.
era: The book covers roughly 850 to 560 BC, when God's people were split into two kingdoms: Israel in the north, with its capital at Samaria, and Judah in the south, ruled from Jerusalem by kings descended from David. Great empires pressed in on them. Assyria conquered Israel in 722 BC, and Babylon later destroyed Jerusalem and its temple. The book's last event, around 561 BC, shows it was completed during the exile.

notes.3:4: A Moabite inscription known as the Mesha Stone, found in 1868, records King Mesha's own account of throwing off Israel's rule.
notes.8:7: Assyrian inscriptions also mention Hazael, describing him as a man of no royal family, which matches his seizing the throne of Aram, the kingdom based at Damascus.
notes.9:14: An Aramean inscription found at Tel Dan, probably set up by Hazael, claims credit for killing Joram and Ahaziah; scholars debate how it fits with this account.
notes.10:29: An Assyrian monument called the Black Obelisk shows Jehu or his envoy bowing and paying tribute to King Shalmaneser III around 841 BC.
notes.14:23: The prophets Amos and Hosea preached in Israel during Jeroboam II's long, prosperous reign.
notes.15:1: Azariah is also called Uzziah; the prophet Isaiah dates his call to the year this king died, around 740 BC.
notes.15:17: Pul is the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III, whose own records list Menahem of Samaria among the kings paying him tribute.
notes.15:27: Tiglath-pileser III's records claim that after Pekah was overthrown, the Assyrian king himself placed Hoshea on Israel's throne.
notes.15:32: The prophets Isaiah and Micah were active in Judah around Jotham's reign.
notes.16:1: This crisis, around 734 BC, is the setting of the prophet Isaiah's meeting with King Ahaz described in Isaiah 7.
notes.17:1: Samaria fell around 722 BC; the Assyrian king Sargon II later claimed in his inscriptions to have captured it and deported its people.
notes.17:24: Jewish tradition traced the later Samaritans partly to these resettled peoples, though the Samaritans themselves trace their roots to the old northern tribes.
notes.18:13: This invasion took place in 701 BC; Sennacherib's own annals describe the campaign and boast of shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem.
notes.18:17: Lachish, Sennacherib's base, was besieged and taken; carved stone panels in his palace at Nineveh show the siege. Isaiah 36–37 tells this same story.
notes.19:35: Sennacherib's murder, told at the end of this passage, is also recorded in a Babylonian chronicle, which says he was killed by his son in a rebellion in 681 BC, about twenty years after this campaign.
notes.20:12: Merodach-baladan was a Babylonian leader who repeatedly rebelled against Assyria, so his envoys may have been seeking allies.
notes.20:20: Hezekiah's water tunnel still runs beneath Jerusalem; an inscription carved by its diggers was discovered inside it in 1880.
notes.21:1: Assyrian records list Manasseh of Judah among the subject kings who sent tribute and building materials to Assyrian rulers.
notes.22:1: The prophets Jeremiah and Zephaniah began their work during Josiah's reign, which started around 640 BC.
notes.22:8: This discovery came around 622 BC; many scholars think the scroll found was some form of the book of Deuteronomy.
notes.23:28: In 609 BC Pharaoh Necho was marching to help the failing Assyrian empire against the rising power of Babylon when Josiah confronted him.
notes.23:36: Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC, bringing Judah under Babylonian control; Jeremiah 36 tells of Jehoiakim burning the prophet's scroll.
notes.24:8: A Babylonian chronicle dates this capture of Jerusalem to early 597 BC; the prophet Ezekiel was among those taken to Babylon.
notes.24:18: Throughout Zedekiah's reign the prophet Jeremiah urged surrender to Babylon, as the book of Jeremiah records.
notes.25:8: Jerusalem and its temple fell in 586 BC (some date it 587); the book of Lamentations traditionally mourns this destruction.
notes.25:22: Jeremiah 40–43 tells this episode more fully, including the prophet himself being taken to Egypt afterwards.
notes.25:27: Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk) began ruling around 562 BC. Years earlier, Babylonian ration tablets already listed Jehoiachin as king of Judah and recorded food allowances for him and his sons while he was a captive.
